Title: Chemicals used to make CE cards...

Messages.Author: Shawn D
Messages.Body:
Ok. Here in St Louis, MO , we had our first taste of the
Camarilla Edition by playing a sealed deck deck games.

Do you wanna know what my very first impression of
the cards was?

It wasn't the looks or playability. The first comment
out of my mouth was, "Damn. These cards smell like
chemicals." A few others noticed the smell but not much
else was said.

About fourty-five minutes into the game, I started
getting a massive frontal headache and soon after
started geting nauseated and a few shakes as well.

I know what you're about to say and I'll agree with
you : there is no evidence the cards caused my
symptoms. However, I speculated that perhaps they
MAY be the cause. One of the other players I played
with also mentioned getting a mild headache after
playing for a while. Others had no symptoms. At the
beginning of the second game, I could again get good
wafes of the noxious odor when shuffling my cards.

While I'm not going to directly corrolate the chemicals
with my symptoms, the main jist of this post is this:

Has anyone else had adverse health effects upon playing
with the cards?

Again, not pointing evidence-less fingers. Just asking.

Otherwise, I was somewhat OK with the cards usability.
Not really happy with some of the design decisions
though and I was rather sad because of the somewhat dismall
mix of cards in the precon Nossie starter I played with.
I was happy enough to pull some Praxis Siezure's, votes,
and a Giant's Blood from the boosters though to make the
deck a bit more playable.

Thanks.

-Shawn D

Messages.Author: Creature
Messages.Body:
FYI,

I work in a printing company, though not the one that printed these
cards. I can tell you for a fact it is not the ink what causes the
smell. Cards are covered in an Ultra-Violet coating to prevent wear
from usage. The finish from this product can be either Matte or Gloss.
This explains the difference between the two Vitels, which were
printed at different times with different coatings. This UV product is
extremely volatile, and therefore smells awful. The product has been
known to cause allergic reactions with our employees (why they wear
gloves and masks when manipulating the coating). Might explain the
headaches. Should tamper down as time goes by and product finishes
drying and evaporating.



Messages.Author: atomweaver
Messages.Body:
lost...@earthlink.net (Shawn D) wrote in message news:<16b7051f.02082...@posting.google.com>...


Wow. This is neat (for me, anyways). I work with the same class of
chemicals as the ones used to make the inks and top coats for card
stock. Since it gives me a chance to talk about what I do in
conjuction with VTES, I'll probably give you more info than you ever
wanted, but read on... until you doze off anyways.

The layman's version
99.95% of all the coatings that go onto paper in the US use a
technology called UV (ultraviolet) curing. Rather than mixing a solid
resin and pigments with a solvent (which is what the paint you buy at
the store is), this technology uses a mixture of resins and liquids
along with a catalyst that reacts when exposed to ultraviolet light.
The catalyst then turns the liquid coating or ink into a solid. The
big differences are #1) emmissions. UV tech produces no appreciable
quantity of volatiles of the sort that irritate your lungs and get you
high (sorry), pollute the environment or make smog. #2) Speed. These
catalysts are fast. Blazing fast. Ludicrously fast. An old solvent
press could run at a pace of about 100 feet per minute through a warm
oven to push the solvent off, but UV tech can run presses at 500 to
700+ feet per minute. The productivity gains with UV are huge. These
sorts of coatings are also what make fiber optic filaments work, and
in those applications, they can run as fast as 1200 _meters_ per
minute!!!

Back to VTES card stock. A very small amount of unreacted UV material
can have significant odor, even though the materials are non hazardous
(there's no known side effects of exposure to the liquid materials,
except for possible allegic reactions among a very small amount of the
population (less than 0.05%). Once solidified, even the allergic
folks can handle them without problems)
Now, if you got a batch of cards that were under-cured, then the odor
is a strong indication. These cards may also wear poorly (keep an eye
on them), and have a finish that is more flatted than other, less
stinky examples from the same set (don't try comparing it to other
sets, its not a valid comparison). This may account for some reports
of very different card "textures" as compared to previous sets.

Personally, I haven't gotten any odor off of the stuff I've opened (3
boxes of boosters, 2 of starters), and I know what to look (I mean
smell) for. If the printer doesn't judiciously attend to his
equipment, though, this problem could be one of a particular day where
the equipment wasn't working well, or a specific lot of top coat or
ink that wasn't prepared properly (most often, deficient in catalyst).

I'm not impressed with White Wolf's printer (I know their business,
and they aren't really doing it that well). They have improved
somewhat since Sabbat War, but I would be looking for a new printer,
If'n I was White Wolf. Too much bad PR from the current one...

Wow. You read this far? Go you...

DaveZ
Atom Weaver
...bringing You environmentally friendly coatings, inks and
adhesives...

Interesting. I honestly haven't done a press check for years, not
since moving my focus to web design, so I'm a bit behind on current
technology. Even if no one else found it interesting, I did!

The current complaints about the ink, the matte finish, typos, and
having three promo cards accidently added to starters got me thinking.
Is White Wolf cutting corners? If so, why?

Consider the problems with the printing, which may indicate they're
using a cheap printer or pushing their printer to squeeze more product
out without increasing the price. Add in the rumors that retailers are
paying a higher price for cards. Now throw in my theory that the real
reason for the design change is to escape paying royalty fees to
Wizards of the Coast for using their copyrighted designs. It all adds
up to White Wolf cutting corners and trying to make more money off of
VTES.

The question is: is it because they just want more money (which is
fine, they're a business, they exist to make money), or is it because
VTES isn't doing well? Does anyone have sales figures from local
stores? As far as I can tell, sales have been okay, but few stores in
St. Louis carry the cards, and even those have some Final Nights and
Bloodlines that aren't moving.

(as a side note, White Wolf only sells directly to stores, not to
internet vendors, which is interesting, as it seems most serious
players buy a lot of their cards over the internet)

JSpektr

cprov...@hotmail.com (Creature) wrote in message news:<83343c7b.02082...@posting.google.com>...

> FYI,

> cards. I can tell you for a fact it is not the ink what causes the
> smell. Cards are covered in an Ultra-Violet coating to prevent wear
> from usage. The finish from this product can be either Matte or Gloss.
> This explains the difference between the two Vitels, which were
> printed at different times with different coatings. This UV product is
> extremely volatile, and therefore smells awful.

...but you know that volatile does not directly equate with stinky.
UV products aren't strictly speaking volatile, they don't evaporate
like acetone or mineral spirits do. Tthat's why you don't need to
clean the press heads (or rolls. Offset? Litho? Gravure?) every
night, and instead can cover them with plastic.

UV acrylates are more like ripe bananas... You can smell 'em in the
kitchen because your nose is sensitive to extremely low concentrations
of that characteristic odor...

> The product has been
> known to cause allergic reactions with our employees (why they wear
> gloves and masks when manipulating the coating). Might explain the
> headaches.

Presonal Protective Equipment is a good start, but you gotta have good
ventilation for the area that they're being used in. Absorption
through the skin is the most frequent method of developing a
sensitization to UV acrylates. Is there a lot of misting of the
product in your shop too? Gotta get good localized suction exhaust to
misting points if there is... Oh, and don't stick your bare hand in
the stuff. Its not a smart thing ;-) A lot of smaller print shops
use UV tech from the eighties, when the allergic reaction problems
were really bad. Newer chemical products developed since don't have
nearly the same level of trouble. Prices on them aren't as low,
though, because the chemical companies need to pay for the development
work done to create these new products.

> Should tamper down as time goes by and product finishes
> drying and evaporating.
>

That'll never happen. Under-cured UV products won't finish their cure
unless re-exposed to UV curing lamps (they're like tanning lamps on
steriods. They'll give you a third degree burn in about a second and
a half). The Smell will go away as the cards are handled and the
small amount of residual liquid is wiped away by the hanlder's
fingers...

Regards
DaveZ

I don't think so - at least, not intentionally.

The matte finish *really is* almost exactly the same as in previous
sets. Take a CE card and hold it up to the light side by side with
a Bloodlines card. If your CE card isn't one of the ones that's
got some roughening or other oddness on it (apparently (possibly)
from uncured UV-finish chemicals) its matteness should be pretty
much identical to that of the Bloodlines card. It was (as far as
I could tell) the promo Marcus Vitels that were anomalously glossy
(and personally I didn't consider that a good thing - they were
even more distinguishable from "regular" cards than the usual
between-set differences).

When I did this comparison, the blacks of the borders looked a
little bit different in terms of saturation/darkness/whatever,
but for the most part the finishes seemed basically the same.

The typos in this set are pretty much on the same level as with
other sets. They fixed a Dark Sovereigns vampire typo (Blythe
Candeleria) but introduced a new one (Brachah). Fixed a VTES
typo (Asylum Hunting Ground) but introduced a new one (Murder of
Crows). There probably haven't been any sets *completely* free
of typos in VTES. I don't really know if other companies manage
typo-free sets, but if so I guess they have more money/people
to devote to proofreading. :-)

Ah, rumors, always a good basis for wild speculation. ;-)

> Now throw in my theory that the real

> Wizards of the Coast for using their copyrighted designs.

This theory is wrong, unless you think WW is lying about their
real reasons for changing the layout for some reason.

The reason they give for the background changes is that the
old background files they inherited from WotC existed as
"complete cards" that only had spaces for (eg) the text and
the symbols.

So, to make any change to the layout at all, they had to redo
the backgrounds.

Now, their choices in designing those new backgrounds may be
debatably good (as the choice to do new layouts in the first
place), but apparently they had to do it. Royalties weren't
involved at all.

As a layman, I'd have thought that they could have somehow
"salvaged" the old graphics and based new background files on
them at least to some extent - take a chunk of old background
and tile it over the entire new-background area, or something
more sophisticated and graphic-designy. :-) But I really have
no idea how feasible that would have been; maybe the old files
weren't modifiable in that way for some reason.

> (as a side note, White Wolf only sells directly to stores, not to
> internet vendors, which is interesting, as it seems most serious
> players buy a lot of their cards over the internet)

How do you mean "only sells directly to stores"? Do they sell
at a discount to stores without going through distributors? I
would have thought that the reason their online sales are set
up the way they are is so that they don't undercut their retailers
(by offering online discounts directly to customers) or their
distributors (by selling discounted product directly to internet
vendors rather than going through the distributors or whatever).

My guess is that it's poor sales, but not necessarily specific to
VTES, just across the board. The economy in general is slumping, and
when people start getting strapped for cash, one of the first things
to go is hobby purchases. This probably has more of an impact on VTES,
whose players are older and do not have the same liquid income as the
younger generation that plays Pokemon, etc. Also, I have been told by
an employee at my local gaming store that relatively speaking the
entire gaming market has dropped, at least compared to the "golden
days" of Magic: The Consumerism when you would cash out several grand
at the end of the day just from selling out on your booster packs.
Things were moderately improved with the rennaisance of D20 Dungeons
and Dragons, but RPG books don't have the sales continuity that CCG's
have, since you only buy them once, and once you have them, they're
all you really need to play.

I hope CE does improve sales for WW, and am releived that they don't
have a larger parent company like Hasbro lording over them and
threatening to cancel product lines if they're not the "next big fad."
I think they have done a superb job managing and improving VTES and
even if something were to happen where the cards were no longer
printed, I would continue to play.

Messages.Author: jspektr
Messages.Body:
"Joshua Duffin" <jtdu...@yahoo.com> wrote in message news:<akip7u$1ij4tp$1...@ID-121616.news.dfncis.de>...

> "jspektr" <jsp...@sprynet.com> wrote in message
> news:196f2577.02082...@posting.google.com...

> > Now throw in my theory that the real

> > reason for the design change is to escape paying royalty fees to
> > Wizards of the Coast for using their copyrighted designs.
>
> This theory is wrong, unless you think WW is lying about their
> real reasons for changing the layout for some reason.

I believe there is a substancial chance their are either lying, or not
telling the whole truth. They are a business, and it is inherent in
most business politics that they distort the truth when disclosing
information to their customers. Considering how reticent White Wolf
has been in the past to reveal even basic information, I do not find
it a stretch to believe they are witholding information about the Cam
redesign.

>
> The reason they give for the background changes is that the
> old background files they inherited from WotC existed as
> "complete cards" that only had spaces for (eg) the text and
> the symbols.

Interesting. That's the first I've heard it. Of course, that still
fails to explain why they decided to make a dramatic layout change; if
they hadn't, the background wouldn't have been a problem and could
have been left as-is.

> So, to make any change to the layout at all, they had to redo
> the backgrounds.

Nonsense. They could have made many minor changes without changing the
backgrounds. They could have moved the discipline symbols, the name at
the top, and even added the verticle bar without changing the
background one bit. If White Wolf disagrees, they are free to send me
the original WoTC files and I will do exactly what I just said. They
can e-mail jsp...@netscape.com (don't get excited, I use that address
for junk mail, and check it irregularly).

> As a layman, I'd have thought that they could have somehow
> "salvaged" the old graphics and based new background files on
> them at least to some extent - take a chunk of old background
> and tile it over the entire new-background area, or something
> more sophisticated and graphic-designy. :-) But I really have
> no idea how feasible that would have been; maybe the old files
> weren't modifiable in that way for some reason.

It would have been laughably easy, if it was even really necessary.
I've recreated more from less in my professional work (the best was
when I had a photo of a client next to his partner, and he had me
erase the partner and recreate from scratch that entire side of his
face and body. It was indestinquishable from a normal photo when I was
done. If I could pull that off, I daresay they can get out the clone
tool in Photoshop and fill in the blanks on the VTES backgrounds).

Even if they decided that was too difficult, they could have created
something at least somewhat similar to the existing backgrounds,
making it less of a jarring change. The fact that they didn't makes me
suspect there is a reason for it, and I currently think avoiding
royalty fees is a good potential reason. I'm not saying that's what's
going on for certain, just that it seems to make sense to me.

>
> > (as a side note, White Wolf only sells directly to stores, not to
> > internet vendors, which is interesting, as it seems most serious
> > players buy a lot of their cards over the internet)
>
> How do you mean "only sells directly to stores"? Do they sell
> at a discount to stores without going through distributors? I

Yes.

> would have thought that the reason their online sales are set
> up the way they are is so that they don't undercut their retailers
> (by offering online discounts directly to customers) or their
> distributors (by selling discounted product directly to internet
> vendors rather than going through the distributors or whatever).
>

If you are a store with a physical storefront, they will sell directly
to you at a discount. If you are an internet-only store, you must buy
your cards from another distributor like Diamond. All this information
is available on the White Wolf website.

JSpektr
